newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says bone fractures are costly to Medicare.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says bone fractures are costly to Medicare.

text.p: Bone fractures among the elderly, often involving the hip, accounted for three percent of all Medicare expenditures, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said bone fractures cost the Medicare program $4.2 billion during a one-year period from July 1991 to June 1992. Hip fractures were associated with $2.9 billion in costs. The federal Medicare budget in 1992 was $138.3 billion.
About 850,000 people aged 65 and older suffer from fractures every year. Total medical care costs for fractures among older adults totaled $13.8 billion in 1995.

"Excess costs to Medicare for fracture treatment are likely to increase steadily" as the American population ages, the CDC said. The number of people 65 and older is projected to increase from 32 million in 1990 to 51.5 million by 2020.

Osteoporosis, a condition that results in decreased bone density, is a major cause of fractures among the elderly, the CDC said. Fractures are more common among women because they have lower peak bone density and lose bone more rapidly than men. Bone fractures occur more often among whites than blacks.

The elderly can reduce their chance of bone fractures by ensuring adequate dietary intake of calcium, engaging in regular weight-bearing physical activity and avoiding smoking and excess alcohol consumption, the CDC said.
